title: Osteoporosis in Older Adults: Fracture Risk, Falls, and Treatment Sequencing
bottomLine: Osteoporosis care prevents fractures, not just low BMD. Estimate fracture risk using age, prior fragility fracture, falls, BMD and secondary causes, then combine exercise/falls/nutrition with pharmacotherapy when risk justifies it; medication choice and duration require renal, dental, calcium and long-term sequencing considerations.
recognize: A recent fragility fracture predicts high near-term fracture risk and should trigger secondary prevention.
Vertebral fractures may be clinically silent and present as height loss or kyphosis.
differentiate: BMD is one risk input; normal calcium does not exclude osteoporosis and a T-score alone does not capture all fracture risk.
Falls and sarcopenia amplify fracture risk independently of BMD.
assessment: Assess prior fractures, falls, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, family history, weight loss, mobility, calcium/vitamin D intake, renal disease and secondary causes.
workup: Use Canada-specific FRAX/BMD and targeted secondary-cause testing according to Osteoporosis Canada guidance; image for suspected vertebral fracture when indicated.
management: Use weight-bearing/resistance/balance exercise, fall prevention and adequate nutrition, plus first-line bisphosphonate or other therapy according to fracture risk and contraindications.
Plan therapy duration/holiday or transition explicitly rather than indefinite unreviewed treatment.
medicationSafety: Review renal suitability, hypocalcemia and dental/jaw risk; denosumab discontinuation requires antiresorptive transition because rebound vertebral fractures can occur.
counselling: Explain absolute fracture risk and the role of falls/strength, not only the BMD result.
followUp: Reassess fractures, adherence, falls and treatment duration at meaningful intervals.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab without a transition plan or treating a number while ignoring recurrent falls.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis treatment follows fracture risk and a long-term medication sequence.

title: Vision and Hearing Loss in Older Adults: Sensory Function Is a Safety Intervention
bottomLine: Sensory loss can masquerade as cognitive decline, worsen falls, isolation and delirium, and reduce medication/self-care safety. Screen functionally, identify reversible/urgent causes and ensure hearing/vision aids actually work in daily life rather than documenting impairment without intervention.
recognize: Hearing loss can present as withdrawal or apparent confusion; cataract, macular degeneration and glaucoma affect different aspects of vision.
Sudden unilateral hearing or vision loss is not normal aging.
differentiate: Delirium/dementia should not be diagnosed without ensuring the person can hear and see the assessment.
Gradual presbycusis differs from sudden sensorineural hearing loss requiring urgent evaluation.
assessment: Ask functional hearing/vision problems, falls/driving, device use, ototoxic drugs, eye pain/visual field symptoms and ability to manage medications.
workup: Use office hearing/vision screening and audiology/optometry/ophthalmology referral; urgent assessment for sudden loss, painful red eye or retinal/vascular symptoms.
management: Optimize corrective lenses/hearing aids, communication environment and lighting, and treat reversible ear/eye disease.
medicationSafety: Review ototoxic medications and ensure medication labels/instructions are accessible.
redFlags: Sensory loss causing unsafe medication/driving errors
counselling: Normalize assistive devices as independence tools rather than markers of decline.
followUp: Confirm devices are obtained, fitted and used and reassess function.
examTrap: Calling an older adult cognitively impaired before correcting severe hearing loss during the assessment.
oneLinePearl: Better hearing and vision can be delirium, falls and autonomy prevention.

title: Driving Safety Assessment: Function, Cognition, Vision, and Jurisdictional Duty
bottomLine: Driving safety is a functional-risk assessment, not an age cutoff. Evaluate cognition, vision, motor function, syncope/seizure, medications and observed driving concerns, know provincial/territorial reporting law, and use formal road/on-road assessment when office findings cannot answer the question.
recognize: Crashes, getting lost, caregiver concern, impaired visuospatial/executive function, syncope and medication sedation are safety signals.
A dementia diagnosis alone does not determine the exact day driving becomes unsafe; severity/function matter.
differentiate: Voluntary driving retirement differs from legally mandated reporting/licence action.
Cognitive screening score alone neither proves nor excludes driving fitness.
assessment: Ask recent collisions/near misses, navigation, vision, limb/neck function, cognition, syncope/seizure, sleepiness, alcohol and sedating medications; obtain collateral when appropriate.
workup: Use vision/cognitive/functional tests and formal driving assessment where available; investigate medical causes such as syncope before clearance.
management: Restrict/stop driving when risk is clearly unacceptable and comply with jurisdictional reporting duties; use conditional/reassessment or specialized driving evaluation for uncertain cases.
Plan alternative transportation to reduce isolation.
medicationSafety: Review benzodiazepines, opioids, antihistamines and other sedating/impairing drugs.
counselling: Discuss driving as a safety/function issue and explain reporting obligations transparently.
followUp: Document advice/reporting and revisit function if driving continues conditionally.
examTrap: Clearing or banning driving from a MMSE/MoCA score alone without functional and legal context.
oneLinePearl: Driving fitness is functional, medical and jurisdictional—not chronological.

title: Elder Abuse: Private Inquiry, Capacity, Safety, and Legal Duties
bottomLine: Elder abuse may be physical, psychological, sexual, financial or neglect. Create private safe conditions, assess immediate danger and decision-making capacity, document objectively and follow jurisdictional reporting duties; a capable adult generally retains choices unless specific legal/safety exceptions apply.
recognize: Unexplained injuries, fearfulness, poor hygiene, medication withholding, financial changes, caregiver control and repeated delay in care can raise concern.
Dependence, isolation and cognitive impairment increase vulnerability but do not prove abuse.
differentiate: Self-neglect, caregiver burnout and intentional abuse require different interventions but can coexist.
Capacity is decision-specific; dementia does not automatically mean incapacity.
assessment: Interview privately, use professional interpreters, assess immediate safety, injuries, finances, medications, food/housing, coercion, caregiver stress, capacity and supports.
workup: Use injury/forensic/medical testing as clinically indicated and social-work/legal consultation for complex capacity/safety issues.
management: Address urgent danger, offer advocacy/community/shelter/legal resources and report according to local adult-protection/LTC statutes when required.
Respect capable-adult autonomy while documenting risk and safety planning.
medicationSafety: Consider medication theft/withholding or over-sedation as possible abuse mechanisms.
redFlags: Financial exploitation causing loss of essentials
counselling: Validate concerns and explain confidentiality/reporting limits before action when possible.
followUp: Use safe contact methods and coordinate services without increasing risk.
examTrap: Automatically calling police after every disclosure despite a capable adult’s wishes and no mandatory trigger—or ignoring abuse because the caregiver seems attentive.
oneLinePearl: Elder-abuse care balances safety, autonomy, capacity and jurisdictional duty.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada elder/family violence resources

title: Advance Care Planning: Values Before the Crisis, Consent in the Present
bottomLine: Advance care planning explores values, priorities and future decision-makers before a crisis; it is not the same as obtaining present consent for a specific treatment. Clarify goals, likely illness trajectories and who will speak if capacity is lost, using provincial/territorial legal terminology and documentation.
recognize: Serious chronic illness, frailty, recurrent hospitalization and cognitive decline create high value for early planning.
Preferences can change and should be revisited.
differentiate: Advance directives/plans guide future decisions; a capable patient’s current informed decision takes priority now.
Goals-of-care discussion is broader than a code-status checkbox.
assessment: Assess understanding, capacity, values, unacceptable health states, tradeoffs, substitute decision-maker structure and family/cultural context.
workup: No medical test determines goals; prognosis and treatment-option evidence should be as accurate as possible.
management: Document values and legal decision-maker information, communicate across care settings and revisit after major health changes.
medicationSafety: Use goals to reconsider preventive/low-benefit medications and treatment burden.
counselling: Frame planning as preserving autonomy rather than predicting death.
followUp: Ensure plans are accessible across settings and updated over time.
examTrap: Treating a prior advance plan as consent for a specific current intervention despite a capable patient expressing a different choice.
oneLinePearl: Advance care planning records values for future decisions; current capacity governs current consent.

title: Palliative Care in Geriatrics: Symptom Relief, Goals, and Function Alongside Disease Treatment
bottomLine: Palliative care is appropriate alongside disease-directed treatment when serious illness causes symptom, decision or caregiver burden. Treat pain, dyspnea, nausea, constipation, anxiety and delirium while aligning investigations/medications with goals; palliative care is not synonymous with imminently dying or stopping all treatment.
recognize: Recurrent hospitalization, progressive frailty, advanced organ disease, cancer/dementia and caregiver distress can indicate palliative needs.
Symptoms are multidimensional and require non-drug plus medication strategies.
differentiate: Palliative care can begin early; end-of-life care is a later phase for some patients.
Opioids used appropriately for pain/dyspnea are not equivalent to euthanasia or MAID.
assessment: Assess symptoms, function, prognosis understanding, goals, caregiver burden, spiritual/cultural needs, medications and preferred place of care.
workup: Order tests only when results are likely to improve comfort or a goal-concordant outcome.
management: Use evidence-based symptom therapy, deprescribe low-benefit burden, coordinate home/hospice/community resources and prepare anticipatory plans for predictable crises.
medicationSafety: Dose opioids/other drugs to renal/hepatic function and prior exposure; prevent constipation and monitor sedation/delirium.
redFlags: New reversible emergency inconsistent with current plan
counselling: Explain that palliative care adds support and does not require abandoning useful disease treatment.
followUp: Reassess symptoms/goals frequently and communicate changes across transitions.
examTrap: Withholding palliative care until the final days because disease-directed treatment is still occurring.
oneLinePearl: Palliative care is added according to need, not prognosis alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian hospice palliative care practice resources

title: Hypertension in Older Adults: Cardiovascular Benefit Without Orthostatic Harm
bottomLine: Treat hypertension in healthy older adults using current Canadian targets, but individualize when frailty, orthostatic hypotension, falls or goals of care make intensive systolic treatment unsafe. Home/standardized BP and symptoms matter more than a single office number.
recognize: Older adults often have isolated systolic hypertension and greater orthostatic vulnerability.
White-coat and measurement error remain common.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic BP elevation is not hypertensive emergency without acute target-organ injury.
Orthostatic symptoms/falls can represent treatment harm even when seated BP looks ideal.
assessment: Use standardized BP, orthostatic vitals when relevant, home readings, frailty/falls, renal function/electrolytes, medication adherence and cardiovascular risk.
workup: Confirm persistent hypertension and evaluate secondary causes only when phenotype suggests them.
management: Use lifestyle and guideline-supported therapy; target SBP <130 when tolerated in suitable adults, but use a higher individualized target when frailty/falls/orthostasis/goals require it.
medicationSafety: Monitor potassium/renal function with RAAS/MRA therapy and avoid over-diuresis or stacked hypotensive drugs causing falls.
counselling: Explain that the safest target balances stroke/CV prevention with standing function and symptoms.
followUp: Review standing symptoms, home BP and labs after medication changes.
examTrap: Intensifying medication because seated SBP is 132 despite recurrent orthostatic syncope.
oneLinePearl: In older adults, BP benefit must survive the standing test.

title: Diabetes in Older Adults: Prevent Hypoglycemia, Preserve Function, Individualize Targets
bottomLine: Diabetes targets in older adults depend on function, frailty, dementia, comorbidity and life expectancy. Strictly prevent hypoglycemia in frail/dependent patients, simplify regimens when burden exceeds benefit and avoid chasing low A1C at the cost of falls, confusion, weight loss or caregiver complexity.
recognize: Hypoglycemia may present as falls, confusion or weakness rather than adrenergic symptoms.
Frailty/dementia reduce benefit from intensive long-horizon prevention and increase treatment harm.
differentiate: Healthy independent older adults may use usual targets; frail/dependent/end-of-life patients require less stringent symptom-focused goals.
A low A1C can represent overtreatment rather than success.
assessment: Assess function/cognition, hypoglycemia, meal reliability, renal function, weight, falls, medication-management ability, caregiver support and goals.
workup: Use A1C/CGM/SMBG only to answer treatment questions; avoid relying on A1C when inaccurate or at end of life when it does not guide care.
management: Prefer low-hypoglycemia therapy, de-intensify insulin/sulfonylurea burden when appropriate and simplify schedules/device demands.
Maintain cardiorenal-protective therapy when benefit aligns with health status/goals.
medicationSafety: Sulfonylureas/insulin increase hypoglycemia risk; renal decline changes many drug/insulin requirements.
counselling: Frame relaxed targets as safer individualized care, not treatment failure.
followUp: Track symptoms, hypoglycemia, function and caregiver burden after simplification.
examTrap: Increasing insulin to push a frail adult with recurrent lows from A1C 7.8% to a younger-adult target.
oneLinePearl: In frail older adults, avoiding hypoglycemia often matters more than lowering A1C further.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guideline — Diabetes in Older People

title: Heart Failure in Older Adults: Congestion, Frailty, Kidney Function, and Goals
bottomLine: Heart failure care in older adults still uses evidence-based disease-modifying therapy, but titration must integrate congestion, perfusion, renal function, potassium, orthostasis, frailty, cognition and goals. Dyspnea/edema are not automatically HF and aggressive diuresis/vasodilation can trade congestion for falls or AKI.
recognize: Orthopnea, edema, JVP and rapid weight gain support congestion; low-output features include hypotension, cool extremities, oliguria and confusion.
Older adults often have multimorbidity and HFpEF.
differentiate: Venous disease, renal/hepatic disease, lung disease and medications can cause edema/dyspnea.
BNP/NT-proBNP is influenced by age, AF, renal function and obesity.
assessment: Assess congestion/perfusion, orthostasis, weight, renal function/electrolytes, rhythm, medications, falls, cognition/adherence, nutrition and goals.
workup: Use ECG, labs and echo to define phenotype and precipitant; investigate ischemia/infection/arrhythmia according to presentation.
management: Use phenotype-appropriate guideline therapy, diuretics for congestion and slow coordinated titration when frailty/orthostasis/renal vulnerability limits pace.
Escalate pulmonary edema, shock, ischemia or severe AKI.
medicationSafety: Monitor renal function/potassium/BP with RAAS/ARNI/MRA/SGLT2 therapy and avoid NSAIDs when possible.
Do not stop all disease-modifying therapy solely because of age.
counselling: Use simple daily weight/symptom/action plans and involve caregivers when desired.
followUp: Early review after decompensation/med changes and close transitions.
examTrap: Withholding foundational HF therapy because the patient is 86 without considering function, goals and tolerance—or over-diuresing into orthostatic AKI.
oneLinePearl: Treat heart failure evidence, but titrate to the older person’s reserve.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart failure guidance

title: Cognitive Impairment Screening: Screen With a Question, Diagnose With History and Function
bottomLine: Cognitive screening is useful when concern exists; it is not a standalone dementia diagnosis. Interpret results with education/language/sensory context, collateral history and function, and exclude delirium/depression/medications before labelling chronic neurocognitive disease.
recognize: Missed medications, finances, navigation or declining IADLs may reveal cognitive impairment before a high screening score becomes obvious.
High education can mask deficits; low education/language difference can lower scores without dementia.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating; depression and sensory impairment can reduce performance.
Capacity is decision-specific and is not determined by a cognitive score.
assessment: Ask patient/collateral about trajectory and IADLs, mood, sleep, medications, hearing/vision and safety.
workup: Use validated tools with appropriate interpretation and targeted labs/imaging when indicated.
management: If abnormal, proceed to full cognitive/functional diagnostic assessment and address reversible contributors/safety.
medicationSafety: Review anticholinergic/sedative burden before attributing impairment to dementia.
counselling: Explain screening as one piece of evidence, not a label.
examTrap: Declaring incapacity because the MoCA is low.
oneLinePearl: Cognitive screens measure performance; dementia diagnosis requires decline and function.

title: Functional Assessment Tools: Measure What the Person Can Actually Do
bottomLine: ADLs, IADLs, gait/mobility and frailty measures translate disease into real-world function. Use them to establish baseline, identify assistance needs, plan rehabilitation/support and monitor change; do not mistake a tool score for a complete capacity or goals-of-care assessment.
recognize: IADL loss often precedes basic ADL dependence.
Function depends on environment, assistive devices and available support, not disease alone.
differentiate: Disability and frailty overlap but are distinct; capacity is decision-specific and not equal to ADL dependence.
assessment: Assess bathing/dressing/toileting/transfers/feeding plus medications, finances, shopping, cooking, transport, communication and mobility.
workup: Select validated tools appropriate to setting and reason; observe performance when history is uncertain.
management: Use OT/PT/home care, devices/environmental modification and caregiver supports targeted to identified deficits.
medicationSafety: Review medication burden when functional decline follows a drug change.
counselling: Frame tools as support-planning instruments, not tests the person passes or fails.
followUp: Repeat when health or supports change and use trend to guide care level.
examTrap: Using an ADL score to declare someone incapable of making medical decisions.
oneLinePearl: Function tools show what support is needed; they do not decide autonomy by themselves.

title: Transitions of Care for Older Adults: Medication, Function, Results, and Named Ownership
bottomLine: Transitions are high-risk clinical events. Reconcile medications, communicate baseline/new function and cognition, identify pending results and follow-up owners, ensure equipment/home supports and give patient/caregiver a usable plan; a discharge summary without closed-loop ownership is not a safe transition.
recognize: Older adults are vulnerable to medication duplication/omission, delirium persistence, deconditioning and missed results after hospital/LTC transitions.
Caregiver capacity may change during an admission.
differentiate: Medication reconciliation is not copying the pre-admission list; every change needs indication/status.
A referral sent is not a referral completed.
assessment: Compare pre/post function/cognition, meds, mobility, continence, nutrition, wound/device needs, caregiver support, home access and understanding.
workup: List pending labs/imaging/pathology and assign named responsibility/timing.
management: Provide reconciled regimen, follow-up appointments/criteria, equipment/home-care services, red flags and direct handoff for high-risk issues.
medicationSafety: Stop duplicates, clarify held/restarted meds and verify renal-dose/anticoagulation/insulin changes.
counselling: Use teach-back and a simplified written plan.
followUp: Early post-discharge contact for high-risk patients and confirmation of pending results/services.
examTrap: Discharging with two anticoagulants because hospital and community medication lists were simply combined.
oneLinePearl: A safe transition names what changed, what is pending, and who owns each next step.

title: Long-Term Care: Frailty-Aware Treatment, Avoidable Transfers, Comfort, and Team Care
bottomLine: Long-term-care decisions should integrate baseline function/cognition, goals, infection/fall/delirium risk, medication burden and facility resources. Avoid automatic hospital transfer or low-value testing when safe on-site care matches goals—but never use LTC residence to dismiss reversible emergencies.
recognize: Residents often have frailty/dementia and atypical infection presentations.
Transfers themselves can cause delirium, deconditioning and care discontinuity.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria or nonspecific decline is not automatically UTI.
Comfort-focused goals do not mean untreated pain, dyspnea or reversible distress.
assessment: Establish baseline, goals/resuscitation plan, current change, hydration, pain, meds, falls, skin, nutrition, devices and available on-site diagnostics/support.
workup: Order tests that can change goal-concordant management; avoid routine urine cultures/labs for nonspecific changes without a clinical question.
management: Treat appropriate acute/chronic disease on site when safe, use hospital transfer for conditions requiring capabilities/goals not available locally, and maintain palliative symptom access.
Use interdisciplinary medication review, falls/skin/nutrition prevention and infection stewardship.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antipsychotics/restraints for behavioural symptoms and monitor high-risk sedative/hypoglycemia/anticoagulant regimens.
redFlags: Unsafe facility capability for needed care
counselling: Discuss likely benefits/burdens of transfer/treatment with resident/substitute decision-maker using current goals.
followUp: Review after acute events/transfers and update care plans/goals.
examTrap: Sending every nonspecific decline to hospital—or refusing transfer for a treatable emergency simply because the patient lives in LTC.
oneLinePearl: LTC care matches treatment intensity to goals and capability, not residence alone.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Long Term Care Recommendations
